newsitem.title: VATICAN: Anglicans, Catholics to consult on future course.
newsitem.headline: Anglicans, Catholics to consult on future course.

text.p: Pope John Paul and Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey said on Thursday women priests had created a serious problem between their Churches and called for fresh consultations on how it would affect future dialogue.

"The obstacle to reconciliation caused by the ordination of women as priests and bishops in some provinces of the Anglican Communion has also become increasingly evident, creating a new situation," the two said in a common declaration.
"In view of this it may be opportune at this stage in our journey to consult further about how the relationship between the Anglican Communion and the Catholic Church is to progress".
It was issued at the end of Carey's first official visit to the Vatican, where he met the Pope on Tuesday and Thursday.
In a series of speeches and statements during the visit, both held their ground on issues dividing their Churches, with each asking the other to understand his position.

The declaration was issued after the two worshipped together at the Rome church of San Gregorio al Celio, from where St Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, set out for England 1,400 years ago.
Carey and the Pope wore full ceremonial garb at the vespers, each bearing signs of the authority of their respective offices.
The common declaration did not say what form the consultation would take although it stressed that a 30-year-old dialogue on other theological matters would continue.
"We have agreed to convene a meeting to review our past progress and future agendas," Carey told a news conference before the vespers service with the Pope.
At several points during Carey's three-day visit both he and the Pope underscored their Churches' commitment to continue dialogue aimed at eventual unity despite formidable obstacles.
"We simply have to trust God for the future," Carey said at the news conference.

"The ordination of women to the priesthood is not the only problem. There are many other issues that we have to look at," Carey added, listing differences over papal primacy, infallibility and the Virgin Mary.
The Vatican says the Catholic Church does not have the authority to ordain women because Christ chose only men as his apostles in an act that showed divine will.
A few Anglican bishops, several hundred priests and several thousand worshippers have converted to Rome over the issue.
The first women were ordained in the Church of England, mother church of Anglicanism, in 1994, four years after Carey was elected the Communion's spiritual leader.
The common declaration said both sides sorely wanted "the grace of reconciliation" that would eventually lead to visible unity between the Churches, which spilt in 1534.

In his sermon at the vespers service, the 76-year-old Pope specifically mentioned the conflict over women priests, saying it had underscored a need for an understanding over doctrinal teaching authority in an eventually unified Church.
The Pope restated his willingness to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the papacy for the sake of unity.
But he also restated that he and future Roman Pontiffs would not settle for a symbolic papacy lacking the essential authority of the papal ministry.

The Church of England was founded when King Henry VIII issued an act denying papal jurisdiction and broke with Rome over the refusal by Pope Clement VII to grant him a marriage annulment so that he could wed Anne Boleyn.
